x: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Commentary on Surah "al-Fil" (The Elephant)
The discussion on the interpretation of the words of the Almighty, Mighty and Majestic:
h

Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? (1) Did He not make their plot go astray? (2) And He sent against them birds in flocks (3) striking them with stones of baked clay (4) and made them like eaten straw (5)

Abu Ja'far (may God have mercy on him) said: The Exalted says to His Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: Have you not looked, Muhammad, with the eye of your heart, and so seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant, who came from Yemen intending to destroy the Ka'ba - the Abyssinians, whose chief was Abraha al-Ashram the Abyssinian?
h
Did He not make their plot go astray?
He says: Did He not make the endeavor of the Abyssinians, the companions of the elephant, to destroy the Ka'ba
h
go astray
? That is: He led them astray from what they intended and attempted of its destruction.
And His words:
h
And He sent against them birds in flocks
. [The Exalted says: And your Lord sent against them birds, scattered,]
n
following one another from various directions. It is a collective plural with no singular, like al-shamatit
n
and al-'abadid
n
and the like. Abu 'Ubayda
n
Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna claimed that he had never seen anyone assign it a singular. Al-Farra'
n

said: I have not heard anything from the Arabs regarding its singular. He said: Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi, who was trustworthy, claimed that he heard that its singular is "iyyala". He said: And al-Kisa'i used to say: I heard the grammarians say: "ibbawl", like "'ijjawl". He said: And I have heard some grammarians say that its singular is "ibbil".
The people of interpretation said something similar to what we have said regarding the ababil.
Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father told me, saying: My uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas,

. He said: They are those that follow one another.

. He said: They are diverse, successive, gathered together

Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, from Qatada, who said:

. He says: Successive, one following in the trail of another.

m: . He said: The ababil are the diverse ones, coming from here and coming from there, reaching them from every place]
. It is mentioned that they were birds that came out
of the sea, and some of them said: They came from the direction of the sea. Then they differed regarding their description.

x: Some of them said: They were white.
Others said: They were black.
Others said: They were green, with beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

c: Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya told us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Muhammad ibn Sirin
m: . He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: They are birds, and they were birds with beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

c: Al-Hasan ibn Khalaf al-Wasiti narrated to me, saying: Waki' and Rawh ibn 'Ubada told us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas,
Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' told us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn 'Abbas,
Ya'qub narrated to us, saying: Hushaym told us, saying:
m: informed us, from 'Ikrima regarding His words:
. He said: They were green birds that came out of the sea, with heads like the heads of predators

c: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr:
m: . He said: They are black sea birds, with stones in [their beaks and claws]

c: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran told us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr:
m: . He said: Black sea birds, with stones in their claws and beaks. He said: Mihran told us, from Kharija, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: They have beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

c: Yahya ibn Talha al-Yarbu'i narrated to us, saying: Fudayl ibn 'Iyad told us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr
m: . He said: Green birds with yellow beaks, going back and forth against them

c: Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' told us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said:
m: Black birds carrying stones in their claws and beaks

x: And His words:
h
striking them with stones of baked clay
. The Exalted says: These ababil birds that God sent against the companions of the elephant strike the companions of the elephant with stones of sijjil. We have already explained the meaning of
h
sijjil
in another place
n
, but we will mention here some of what has been said about it, from the sayings of those we did not mention there.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran told us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas:
Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dhari' narrated to me, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas:
m: striking them with stones of sijjil

c: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas:
Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dhari' narrated to me, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' told us, from 'Umara ibn Abi Hafsa, from 'Ikrima
m: striking them with stones of sijjil

c: Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Shu'ba told us, from Sharqi, who said:
m: striking them with stones of sijjil

c: Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Husayn informed us, from 'Ikrima, who said:
m: They were striking them with stones that they had with them. He said: Whoever of them was hit, smallpox broke out on him. He said: It was the first day on which smallpox was seen. He said: It was not seen before that day, nor after it

c: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran told us, from Sufyan, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'isha, who said:
m: Abu al-Kanud mentioned: Smaller than a chickpea and larger than a lentil.

c: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'isha, who said:
m: The stones with which they were pelted were larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea. He said: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri told us, saying:

c: Isra'il told us, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'isha, from 'Imran,
Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' told us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said:
m: "Sijjil" in Persian is: sang-u-gil; stone and clay

c: Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' told us, from Isra'il, from Jabir,
m: Ibn Sabit, who said: In the foreign tongue it is: sang-u-gil (1).

c: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada, who said:
m: there were three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, and it kept striking them with them.

c: Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada:
m: . He said: They are of clay

c: Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, who said:
m: They were white birds that came from the direction of the sea, with each bird three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak; it struck nothing without shattering it

c: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying:
m: 'Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ya'qub, that his father informed him that it had reached him that the birds that pelted with the stones were carrying them in their mouths, and that when they dropped them, blisters

x: Others said: The meaning of that is: They strike them with stones from the lowest heaven.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said
m: striking them with stones of sijjil
. He said: The lowest heaven. He said: And the lowest heaven is named Sijjil, and it is the one from which God, Mighty and Majestic, sent down stones upon the people of Lot
. He said: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying:

c: 'Amr ibn al-Harith informed us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal,
m: that it reached him that the birds that pelted with stones were birds that came out of the sea, and that

is the lowest heaven. As for this statement made by Ibn Zayd, we know no basis for its soundness in any report, reason or language; for the names of things are only known through a prevailing language or a report from God, the Exalted. The cause for which God's punishment, the Exalted, befell the companions of the elephant was the march of Abraha the Abyssinian with his army and the elephant toward the Sacred House of God in order to destroy it. And what prompted him to that, according to what Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying:

c: Salama ibn al-Fadl told us, saying: Ibn Ishaq told us,
m: is that Abraha built a church in San'a' - he was a Christian - and called it al-Qullays. Nothing like it was seen in its time anywhere on earth. And he wrote to al-Najashi the king of Abyssinia: I have built for you, O king, a church the like of which has not been built for any king before you, and I will not rest until I divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it. When the Arabs began to talk about Abraha's letter to al-Najashi, a man of the Nasa'a
, one of the Banu Fuqaym, of the Banu Malik, became angry, and set out until he reached al-Qullays and sat in it

, then went out and rejoined his own land. Abraha was informed of that, and said: Who did this? He was told: A man from the people of this House to which the Arabs make pilgrimage, in Mecca, did it, when he heard your saying: I will divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it. He became angry and came and sat in it, meaning: it is not worthy of that. Abraha became angry at that, and swore that he would march on the House and demolish it. With Abraha were men of the Arabs who had come to him seeking his favor; among them Muhammad ibn Khuza'i ibn Hizaba al-Dhakwani, then al-Sulami, with a group of his people, accompanied by a brother of his called Qays ibn Khuza'i. While they were with him, a feast of Abraha's came upon them, and he sent them his food for it; he used to eat testicles. When the food reached the men, they said: By God, if we eat this, the Arabs will keep reviling us for it as long as we live. So Muhammad ibn Khuza'i got up and went to Abraha and said: O king, this is a feast day for us, on which we eat only thighs and hands. Abraha said to him: We shall send you whatever you like; I only honored you with my food because of your standing with me. Then Abraha crowned Muhammad ibn Khuza'i, appointed him over Mudar, and ordered him to travel among the people, calling them to the pilgrimage to al-Qullays, his church that he had built. So Muhammad ibn Khuza'i set out, until he halted in some land of the Banu Kinana - and the people of Tihama had heard of his affair and what he had come for - and they sent against him a man of Hudhayl called 'Urwa ibn Hiyad al-Mulasi. He shot him with an arrow and killed him. With Muhammad ibn Khuza'i was his brother Qays ibn Khuza'i, who fled when his brother was killed and joined Abraha and told him of his killing, which increased Abraha in anger and fury, and he swore that he would raid the Banu Kinana and demolish the House. Then, when Abraha resolved to march on the House, he ordered the Abyssinians, and they got ready and equipped themselves, and he set out with the elephant. The Arabs heard of that and considered it monstrous

, and they saw waging jihad against him as an obligation upon them when they heard that he intended to demolish the Ka'ba, the Sacred House of God. A man who was one of the nobles and kings of the people of Yemen, called Dhu Nafar, came forward, and called his people and whoever of the rest of the Arabs answered him to fight Abraha and wage jihad against him in defense of the House of God and what he intended of its demolition and ruin. Those who would answered him, and he confronted him and fought him, but was defeated and his companions scattered, and Dhu Nafar was taken prisoner, [and was brought]
to him. When he wished to kill him, Dhu Nafar said to him

: O king, do not kill me, for perhaps my remaining with you will be better for you than killing me. So he spared him from death and kept him with him in bonds; Abraha was a forbearing man. Then Abraha went on his way, intending what he had set out for, until, when he was in the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him with the two tribes of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahis, and those who followed him

from the Arab tribes, and fought him; Abraha defeated him and took him prisoner and was brought him, and when he was about to kill him, Nufayl said to him: O king, do not kill me, for I am your guide in the land of the Arabs, and here are my two hands for you over the two tribes of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahis, in hearing and obedience. So he pardoned him and let him go, and he set out with him with him to guide him on the way, until when he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib came out to him with the men of Thaqif and said: O king, we are only your slaves, hearing you and obeying you; you have no disagreement with us, and this temple of ours is not the House you want - meaning al-Lat - what you want is the House in Mecca - meaning the Ka'ba - and we shall send with you someone to guide you. So he passed over them, and they sent with him

Abu Righal. Abraha set out with Abu Righal until he brought him down at al-Mughammis; when he made him halt there, Abu Righal died there, and the Arabs stoned his grave, and it is the grave that people stone at al-Mughammis. When Abraha halted at al-Mughammis, he sent a man of the Abyssinians called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud with a cavalry force of his until he reached Mecca, and drove off to him the property of the people of Mecca, of Quraysh and others, and took from it
two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, who was then the elder of Quraysh and its chief. Quraysh, Kinana, Hudhayl and whoever else

was in the Sanctuary among the rest of the people considered fighting him, but then they realized they had no power against him and gave that up. Abraha sent Hunata al-Himyari to Mecca and said to him: Ask about the chief of this land and their noble, then say to him: The king says to you: I did not come to fight you; I came only to demolish the House. If you do not stand in his way with war, I have no need of your blood; and if he does not want to fight me, bring him to me. When Hunata entered Mecca, he asked about the chief of Quraysh and its noble, and was told

: 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy. He came to him and said to him what Abraha had ordered him, and 'Abd al-Muttalib said to him: By God, we do not want to fight him, and we have no power for that. This is the Sacred House of God, and the house of His intimate friend Abraham, peace be upon him - or as he said - so if He protects it, it is His house and His sanctuary, and if He lets him have it, then by God we have [no defense]
against him. Or as he said to him

. Hunata said to him: Then come along to the king, for he ordered me to bring you to him. So 'Abd al-Muttalib went with him, with some of his sons, until he reached the camp, and asked about Dhu Nafar, who was his friend, and was directed to him, and came to him while he was in his prison, and said: O Dhu Nafar, do you have any help to offer in what has befallen us? Dhu Nafar said to him
: What help can a man offer who is a prisoner in the hands
of a king, awaiting that he will kill him morning or evening?! I have no help to offer in anything of what has befallen you, except that Unays, the keeper

of the elephant, is a friend of mine; I shall send for him and commend you to him, and stress to him your right, and ask him to seek permission for you to see the king so that you may speak to him of what you want, and he may intercede for you with him for good if he is able. He said: That is enough for me. So Dhu Nafar sent for Unays, who came, and said: O Unays, 'Abd al-Muttalib is the chief of Quraysh and the master of the caravans of Mecca; he feeds the people on the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain peaks; and the king has taken two hundred camels of his; so seek permission for him to see him, and benefit him with him as much as you can. He said: I will. So Unays spoke to Abraha and said: O king, this is the chief of Quraysh at your door seeking permission to see you; he is the master of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds the people on the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain peaks; so give him permission to see you, so that he may speak to you of his need, and be good to him. He said: So Abraha gave him permission. 'Abd al-Muttalib was a great man, handsome and imposing; when Abraha saw him, he revered him and honored him too much to have him sit below him, but disliked that the Abyssinians should see him seat him with himself on the throne of his kingdom, so Abraha came down from his throne and sat on his carpet, and seated him with himself on it beside him, then said to his interpreter: Ask him: What is your need of the king?

c: The interpreter told him,
m: and 'Abd al-Muttalib said to him: My need of the king is that he return to me two hundred camels he took from me. When he said that to him, Abraha said to his interpreter: Tell him: You impressed me when I saw you, then I lost regard for you when you spoke to me; do you speak to me about two hundred camels I took from you, and leave a house that is your religion and the religion of your forefathers, which I have come to demolish, and not speak to me about it?! 'Abd al-Muttalib said to him: I am the owner of the camels, and the House has an Owner who will protect it. He said: It will not be protected from me. He said: That is between you and Him
; return my camels to me. It is claimed by some of the people of knowledge that there had gone with 'Abd al-Muttalib to Abraha, when he sent Hunata to him, Ya'mar
ibn Nufatha ibn 'Ali ibn al-Du'il ibn Bakr ibn 'Abd Manat

ibn Kinana, who was then the chief of Kinana, and Khuwaylid ibn Wa'ila al-Hudhali, who was then the chief of Hudhayl, and they offered Abraha a third of the wealth of Tihama on condition that he turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused them, and God knows best. Abraha had returned to 'Abd al-Muttalib the camels he had taken from him, and when they left him, 'Abd al-Muttalib returned to Quraysh and told them the news, and ordered them to leave Mecca and to take refuge in the mountain peaks
and the ravines, fearing for them [the harm of the army]

. Then 'Abd al-Muttalib got up and took hold of the ring of the door, the door of the Ka'ba, and a group of Quraysh stood with him calling on God and asking His help against Abraha and his troops. And 'Abd al-Muttalib, holding the ring of the door of the Ka'ba, said: O Lord, I hope for none but You against them. O Lord, protect Your sanctuary from them. The enemy of the House is whoever is hostile to You. Prevent them from laying waste to Your settlements. And he also said: O God, a man protects his own household, so protect Your own people. Let not their cross and their might, by morning, ever overcome Your might. If You leave them with our qibla, then perhaps it is fitting; the matter is as it seems good to You. And if You do so, it is a matter by which You complete Your work

. You were, when an aggressor came in peace, such that we hoped You would be so to us. So they turned back, gaining nothing but disgrace, and doom destroyed them there. And I have not heard of any viler than men who wanted glory and so violated Your sacred precinct. They dragged along the hosts of their lands and the elephant, to take captive Your dependents. Then 'Abd al-Muttalib let go of the ring of the door of the Ka'ba, and he and those with him of Quraysh went off to the mountain peaks and took refuge in them, waiting to see what Abraha would do in Mecca when he entered it. When morning came, Abraha prepared to enter Mecca, and made ready his elephant and drew up his army; the elephant's name was Mahmud, and Abraha was determined to demolish the House and then return to Yemen. When they directed the elephant, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami came until he stood beside him, then took hold of his ear and said: Kneel, Mahmud, and return safely to where you came from, for you are in the Sacred Land of God. Then he let go of his ear, and the elephant knelt, and Nufayl ibn Habib ran off until he climbed up the mountain, and they beat the elephant to make it stand, but it refused, and they struck its head with the axe
to make it stand, but it refused, so they inserted their hooks into its belly

with them to make it stand, but it refused. They then turned it back toward Yemen and it stood up trotting; they turned it toward Syria and it did the same; they turned it toward the east and it did the same; they turned it toward Mecca and it knelt. And God sent against them birds from the sea like swallows, each bird carrying three stones: one stone in its beak and two in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils, which struck none of them without his perishing, though not all of them were hit. They fled, hurrying along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib to guide them on the road to Yemen. When Nufayl ibn Habib saw what God had sent down upon them of His vengeance, he said: Where is the escape, when God is the pursuer, and al-Ashram the defeated, not the victor. They went out falling along every road and perishing at every watering place. Abraha was afflicted in his body, and they carried him out with them, his fingertips falling
one joint after another; whenever a joint fell, pus followed it, oozing
with matter and blood, until they brought him to San'a', looking like a fledgling bird; and he did not die until his chest split open his chest away from his heart, as they claim

c: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama told us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Ya'qub ibn 'Utba ibn al-Mughira ibn al-Akhnas,
m: that he related that the first time measles and smallpox were seen in the land of the Arabs was that year, and that it was the first time the bitter trees were seen there - al-harmal, al-hanzal and al-'ushar - that year
b.via: Ya'qub ibn 'Utba ibn al-Mughira ibn al-Akhnas

c: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada
m: Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant
, with those with him of the raiders

of the people of Yemen, to the House of God to demolish it, because of a church of theirs that the Arabs had defiled in the land of Yemen. They advanced with their elephant until, when they reached al-Sifah, it knelt; whenever they directed it toward the House of God it laid its chest on the ground, and when they directed it toward their own country it set off trotting. Until, when he was at Nakhla al-Yamaniyya, God sent against them white birds in flocks - and the ababil are the numerous - each [bird of them]

with three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, and they kept striking them with them until God, Mighty and Majestic, made them like eaten straw. He said: Abu Yaksum, who is Abraha, escaped, and whenever he came to a land, some of his flesh fell off, until he reached his people and told them the news, and then died.

x: And His words:
h
and made them like eaten straw

. The Exalted means: God made the companions of the elephant like crops that beasts had eaten and then excreted, so that they dried out and their parts were scattered. He likened the severing of their limbs by the punishment that befell them, and the scattering of the parts of their bodies by it, to the scattering of the parts of the dung produced by the eating of crops. Some have said: The 'asf is the outer husk on the grain of wheat, like a sheath for it, on the outside.
Mention of those who said: What is meant by it is the leaf of the crop.

c: Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: 'Isa told us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us,
m: both from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words:
. He said: The leaf of wheat

c: Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr told us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada:
m: . And I was told from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say:

c: 'Ubayd informed us, saying:
m: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words:

c: Muhammad ibn 'Umara al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: Zurayq ibn Marzuq told us, saying: Hubayra told us, from Salama ibn Nubayt, from al-Dahhak
m: , in Nabataean. And in one report: the subdued.

c: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said
m: and made them like eaten straw
. He said: The leaf of crops and the leaf of greens, when livestock eat it and excrete it, so that it becomes dry rubble

x: Mention of those who said: What is meant by it is the husk of the grain.

c: Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father told me, saying: My uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas:
m: . He said: Wheat is eaten and the wind casts off its 'asf, and the 'asf is what is above the wheat; it is the bark of the wheat

x: Others said something different about it, according to what Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying:

c: Mihran told us, from Abu Sinan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit:
m: . He said: Like food that has been eaten. End of the commentary on Surah "al-Fil".

notes.en: Shamāṭīṭ means separate groups; one says “the cavalry came shamāṭīṭ,” that is, in scattered detachments. Lisān al-ʿArab, root (ش م ط).

notes.en: Al-Zamakhsharī said: “Nafṭ in the Hudhayl dialect means smallpox, which affects children and sheep.” Abū Zayd said: “When fluid forms between skin and flesh, one says nafiṭat, tanfaṭu, nafṭan wa-nafīṭan.” See Tāj al-ʿarūs, root (ن ف ط).
notes.ar: قال الزمخشري: النَّفْط بلغة هذيل: الجدرى يكون بالصبيان والغنم، وقال أبو زيد: إذا كان بين الجلد واللحم ماء قيل: نَفِطَت تنفَط نفطا ونفيطا. ينظر تاج العروس (ن ف ط).

notes.en: A nāsiʾ man and a nasāʾa people were those who disliked having three consecutive sacred months in which they could not raid, since their livelihood depended on raiding. They therefore declared Muḥarram lawful; this was called nasīʾ. Lisān al-ʿArab, root (ن س أ).
notes.ar: رجل ناسئ وقوم نسأة، وذلك أنهم كانوا يكرهون أن يتوالى ثلاثة أشهر حرم لا يغيرون فيها؛ لأن معاشهم كان من الغارة، فيحل لهم شهر المحرم، فذلك الإنساء. ينظر اللسان (ن س أ).

notes.en: Ibn Hishām said: “That is, he introduced something new into it.” Sīrat Ibn Hishām, 1/45.

notes.ar: الشَّعَفة: رأس الجبل. جمعها: شَعَف وشُعوف وشِعاف وشَعَفات. التاج (ش ع ف).

notes.en: M and the printed edition of the author’s history add “and he also said” after this; it is absent from the manuscripts of the history. The preceding verses are in majzūʾ al-kāmil meter, and those that follow are in al-wāfir, except the final line, which is in majzūʾ al-kāmil like the first verses. This last line appears in the author’s history after the first four verses.
notes.ar: بعده في م، ومطبوعة تاريخ المصنف: "وقال أيضا"، وهى ساقطة من نسخ تاريخ المصنف. والأبيات السابقة من مجزوء الكامل والآتية من الوافر، عدا البيت الأخير فهو من مجزوء الكامل كالأبيات الأولى. وقد جاء هذا البيت الأخير في تاريخ المصنف بعد الأربعة الأبيات الأولى.

notes.en: Ṭabarzīn is a saddle axe, a Persian loanword. Al-Jawālīqī said that Persian horsemen carried it with them to fight. Al-Muʿarrab, p. 276.
notes.ar: الطبرزين: فأس السرج؛ فارسي معرب، قال الجواليقي: لأن فرسان العجم تحمله معها يقاتلون به. المعرب ص 276.

notes.en: Marāqq al-baṭn means the lower abdomen and the surrounding delicate area. Lisān al-ʿArab, root (ر ق ق).
notes.ar: مَراقُّ البطن: أسفله وما حوله مما استرقَّ منه. اللسان (ر ق ق).

notes.en: Bazagha damahu means “he made his blood flow.” Lisān al-ʿArab, root (ب ز غ).
notes.ar: بَزَغَ دمه: أسأله. اللسان (ب ز غ).

notes.en: M reads “so it fell.”
notes.ar: في م: "فسقطت".

notes.en: Maththa al-ʿaẓm means the marrow or fat within the bone flowed. Lisān al-ʿArab, root (م ث ث). Al-Suhaylī says in al-Rawḍ al-unuf, 1/273, that the verb may be read with ḍamma or kasra: with ḍamma it is transitive and “pus” is its object; with kasra it is intransitive and “pus” is accusative as a specification, according to most scholars.
notes.ar: مثَّ العظمُ مثًّا: سال ما فيه من الودك. اللسان (م ث ث)، وقال السهيلي في الروض الأنف 1/ 273: تَمُثُّ وتمِثُّ بالضم والكسر، فعلى رواية الضم يكون الفعل متعديًا ونصب "قيحًا" على المفعول، وعلى رواية الكسر يكون غير متعدٍّ ونصب "قيحًا" على التمييز في قول أكثرهم.

notes.en: Sīrat Ibn Hishām, 1/45–54; the author also reported it in his history, 2/130–137. Al-Bayhaqī reported it in Dalāʾil al-nubuwwa, 1/115–121, through Yūnus ibn Bukayr from Ibn Isḥāq.

notes.en: It is the chaff of grain. It may also be a piece cut from meat. Lisān al-ʿArab, root (هـ ب ر).
notes.ar: هو دقاق الزرع. ويحتمل أن يكون من الهبر القَطْع. اللسان (هـ ب ر).

notes.en: S, T1, T2, and T3 read “worn down”; M reads “dung.” The adopted reading agrees with the source cited for the report. Darīn means the remains of pasture vegetation once scattered and fallen to the ground. Al-Nihāya, 2/115. Ibn Kathīr cites the report in his Tafsīr, 8/509.
